items.s: Building permits for new private housing.
items.w: Building permits are listed among the leading indicators that change before the economy turns.

items.s: The prime rate.
items.w: Interest rates, particularly the prime rate, change only after a trend is already underway.

items.s: The S&P 500 and other stock market indices and averages.
items.w: Stock market indices are an important leading indicator of economic activity and cycles.

items.s: Corporate profits.
items.w: Corporate profits are a lagging indicator, changing after the economy has begun following a trend.

items.s: Layoff rates.
items.w: Layoff rates are leading indicators, unlike the unemployment rate itself, which is a lagging indicator.

items.s: The unemployment rate.
items.w: The unemployment rate lags because it does not turn until cycle trends are already underway.

title: Easing vs Tightening the money supply

items.s: The Fed buys Treasury securities from primary dealers and pays them cash.
items.w: Fed purchases put cash into the banking system, which increases the money supply and lowers rates.

items.s: The Fed raises the reserve requirement so banks must keep more deposits on hand.
items.w: A higher reserve requirement leaves banks less to lend, which tightens the money supply.

items.s: The Fed lowers the discount rate charged to banks.
items.w: Lowering the discount rate is on the Fed’s ease checklist alongside buying securities and lowering reserves.

items.s: The Fed sells securities to primary dealers to curb inflation or an overheating economy.
items.w: Selling securities soaks up cash from dealers, shrinking the money supply and pushing interest rates up.

items.s: The Fed lowers the reserve requirement, letting banks lend more of each deposit.
items.w: A reduced reserve requirement is an expansionary strategy because banks keep fewer funds on deposit.

items.s: Cash leaves the banking system, credit becomes harder to obtain and interest rates rise.
items.w: Removing cash from circulation makes credit harder to obtain, which is the effect of tightening.

items.s: To stimulate growth, increase government spending and reduce taxes.
items.w: Keynesians propose higher spending and lower taxes, which are fiscal tools, to stimulate the economy.

items.s: Variations in the money supply have major influences over national output and price levels.
items.w: Monetarists emphasize the role of the money supply in controlling national output and price levels.

items.s: To control inflation, decrease government spending and increase taxes.
items.w: The Keynesian inflation-control toolkit is fiscal: spend less and tax more to cool demand.

items.s: To control inflation, decrease the amount of money in circulation.
items.w: Monetarists fight inflation by contracting the money supply, not by changing spending or taxes.

items.s: The economy is best controlled through taxation and government spending.
items.w: Keynesian economists believe taxation and government spending are the best way to control the economy.

items.s: Popularized by Milton Friedman, this school stresses the role of central banks.
items.w: Milton Friedman popularized monetarism, which focuses on central banks and the money supply.

items.s: US imports increase because foreign goods are cheaper for US businesses and consumers.
items.w: When the dollar strengthens it buys more foreign currency, so imports become cheaper and rise.

items.s: US exports increase because US goods look more attractive to foreign buyers.
items.w: A weaker dollar makes US goods cheaper abroad, so exports increase.

items.s: The usual result when Fed actions raise US interest rates and investors shift assets into dollars.
items.w: Higher US rates draw investors into dollars, which generally raises the dollar’s foreign exchange value.

items.s: Foreign investment in the US dollar declines.
items.w: Foreign investors are drawn to a strong dollar, so a weakening dollar reduces foreign investment.

items.s: US exports decrease because US goods are expensive for consumers in many foreign countries.
items.w: A strong dollar raises the foreign price of US goods, which restrains exports.

items.s: US imports decline because foreign goods cost American buyers more.
items.w: A weak dollar buys less foreign currency, making imports more expensive and reducing them.

title: Federal funds rate vs Discount rate

items.s: The rate banks charge one another for overnight loans.
items.w: The federal funds rate is the interbank overnight lending rate, not a Fed lending rate.

items.s: The rate the Federal Reserve charges banks and depository institutions for short-term credit.
items.w: The discount rate is the interest rate on credit available from the Fed itself.

items.s: Determined by supply and demand in the market; the Fed does not directly set it.
items.w: The fed funds rate is market-driven, only heavily influenced by open market operations.

items.s: Considered the most volatile interest rate in the market.
items.w: The Knopman Note identifies the market-driven fed funds rate as the most volatile rate.

items.s: A direct tool of the Fed, lowered to ease and raised to tighten the money supply.
items.w: The discount rate is one of the Fed’s three tools, lowered to ease and raised to tighten.

items.s: The higher of these two rates in the order fed funds, discount, broker call, prime.
items.w: The lowest-to-highest ordering places the discount rate above the federal funds rate.
